Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee at its next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That, it is expedient to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act to facilitate and increase the extension of credit to farmers, to authorize the Minister of Finance to purchase additional bonds issued by the board and guaranteed by the government, and to amend' the provisions relating to the constitution of the board, the purchase of capital stock, the rate of interest, the amount of outstanding bonds, and supplementary advances.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CHAIRMANSHIP OF BOARD-APPLICATIONS FOR ARBITRAL TRIBUNALS
speechtext:
I should like to address two questions to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), or possibly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). In view of the fact that the chairmanship of the board of railway commissioners has been vacant, can the government give any information to the house as to when we may expect the appointment of a chairman to be made? If I may put my second question now, though perhaps the minister is not prepared

to give an answer to-day, I should like to ask if any applications have been made by either of the two railways for arbitral boards under the legislation passed two sessions ago and, if so, if consideration is being delayed by reason of the fact that the board has no chairman.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: CHAIRMANSHIP OF BOARD-APPLICATIONS FOR ARBITRAL TRIBUNALS
speechtext:
In regard to the first
question I shall take this as a notice and give the answer to-morrow. In regard to the second question, so far as I know no official indication has been given by either railway of a desire for an arbitral tribunal.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) whether it is the intention of the government to go on immediately with the work in connection with the postal terminal in Montreal or whether the government will content itself with the excavation work?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: If my memory serves me right, last year, in a similar case, I had to request the hon. member for St. James to direct his question to the Minister of Public Works.
Then I will put my question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart). I did not know there was friction in the cabinet to that extent.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask that that observation be withdrawn.
I will put my question to the Minister of Public Works.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

Such an allegation is unwarranted.

Reform Measures-Mr. Pouliot

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The question is one which in the first instance I think might have been directed to the department which has control of the work rather than to the Post Office Department, which really has nothing to do with the construction of the building. The work has not been abandoned; it will be proceeded with in due course.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, January 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Guthrie that the house resolve itself into committee of supply, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King.
Mr. GEORGE W. McPHEE (Yorkton): Mr. Speaker, at eleven o'clock last evening I was discussing the amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), but in view of the definite declaration made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), who was leading the house last evening, that the resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in regard to unemployment insurance would foe proceeded with to-day, and in order to expedite consideration of that resolution. I have no further observations to make at this time.
Mr. JEAN -FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker I should like to dictate to the Hansard reporter a short prefatory note to the so-called social legislation of this government. I am in a privileged position, because I did not listen to the recent speeches delivered over the radio by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), nor have I read them. What I should like to say, however, is that the Prime Minister's political adviser now, Mr. Herridge, the Canadian minister in Washington, is the same gentleman who was his political adviser during the 1930 campaign, when all the humbug promises were made to the Canadian people. This is why I am most doubtful as to the success of this legislation.
I will say more, sir; although my speech will be very short, may I recall some facts to hon. members of the house. Before the
special session of 1930 was called a board was created by this government to study the causes of unemployment. There were some eminent gentlemen on that board, but they sat for only a short time before presenting their recommendations to the government. I remember that one member was Mr. J. H. Fortier. Later we came here for the special session, when we were told that $20,000,000 would cure unemployment. That amount was voted. Was the amount expended that had been put in the estimates by the previous government? It was not. Even that amount of $20,000,000 was not spent by this government. We were told also that if the tariffs were raised it would solve the unemployment problem. Were there many unemployed at that time? No, there were not; there were only a few poor people. One of my hon. friends from the province of Quebec told me that on the Indian reservation in his constituency there were 4,500 people who were always unemployed; they never did work, therefore they were then counted among the unemployed at that time.
Then what happened? After we were told in 1930 that by increasing the tariff we would reduce unemployment the Prime Minister told us that he had obtained the solemn promise of the manufacturers that if given an increase in the tariff they would employ more men at better wages, but later we saw the downfall of all hopes, both inside and outside of this house. Then the Prime Minister went over to the imperial conference with one or two of his colleagues, and what did he do? He wanted a tariff wall raised by England against her ordinary trade with other nations, but he failed, and it was then that Mr. Thomas used the expression "humbug." Then, after that pilgrimage to London which proved a complete failure, the Prime Minister came back here and found that the N.R.A. was the only remedy that would solve the problems which he had created in Canada through his tariffs, in order to please those vultures whom we saw in such large numbers in the corridors of this parliament during the special session of 1930, those profiteers who made so much money at the expense of the Canadian people during the war.
The tariff was raised again and again. I remember that my right hon. leader asked the Prime Minister on how many items the tariff had been raised during the session of 1931, and if my memory serves me aright the right hon. leader of the opposition suggested that it had been raised on two-thirds of the items. If I remember correctly the Prime Minister said it had been raised on one-half

Reform Measures-Mr. Pouliot
the items, or a little more than one-half. What was the result? Each month our trade has decreased so much that now the government is afraid to make a comparison with the figures of the fast year the Mackenzie King government was in power. Their point of comparison is the year 1932, not because there was an imperial conference in that year but because at that time our trade had reached rock bottom. Why? On account of that silly increase in tariff. That is what happened in 1932, after the increase of tariffs in the special session of 1930 and the regular session of 1931.
Sir, I can speak about it, because when your predecessor was in the chair I was sitting at the other end of this chamber, and when he asked if the tariff increases were approved I said "On division." That fact was noted by the correspondent for Le Devoir and the correspondents for other papers. Therefore as I objected to it at the time I now have the right to censure the increases in tariff made since this government has been in power. Not only that: What did this government do? They passed legislation so that tariffs could be increased by order in council, a most absurd procedure, because when a man buys goods from another country he is not sure he will pay the same price when the goods reach Canada. It proved that the N.R.A. suggested and established by this government, which treated walls around the country, was a complete failure. It was just as much a failure, so far as Canada is concerned, as the London tonference of 1930.
It was a complete and utter failure, but this government looked ahead to the imperial conference of 1932 when the representatives were gathered in Canada in order to discuss an economic policy. It is all right for the dominions to meet in London so as to have the same constitutional rights, but when it comes to a business proposition it is most absurd for five or ten parties to meet together in order to have a better chance at business. We know, sir, that a man can make a good business deal only by discussing with the other party. The purchaser and the seller must get together, and this is how agreements have been made in the past. The government renounced the Dunning agreements, abolished them and changed them so as to give place for a silly tariff policy. Then they brought Mr. Baldwin and other gentlemen from other parts of the empire to this very room, thinking that by that procedure the future of Canada would be saved.
Sir, 1932 proved the same as 1931 and 1930. Why? Because there was no preparation of the government's policy. It is a well known fact that Mr. Baldwin was ready to go with-

out signing a piece of paper, without agreeing to any agreements or treaties. However his departure was delayed for one day. When the tables at the Chateau Laurier were groaning with food there were upstairs some English experts who knew their business. They were very intelligent, very clever and well trained and experienced British officials who had their proposals ready. They wanted this government to subscribe to those documents. Finally because this government wanted the scrap of paper with the signatures of English and other British representatives upon it they accepted everything submitted to them. It is especially to be noted that they accepted the creation of a tariff board before which England could lodge its complaints, but we had not the same privilege in England. Those agreements bound Canada hand and foot, but England was free to trade with any other country.
After the agreements of 1932 were signed we heard this government saying throughout the country that the future of Canada would be brilliant, and that Canada had nothing to fear. They said that the agreements had saved the life of our country and that this government was doing so well. That, again, was a failure. So much is that the fact that I remember the Minister of Railways, who knew that, saying in the following session, " Let us wait until the world conference next year. Everything will be settled there, and we will have our trade with all the nations of the world." When on October 12, 1932, the Prime Minister explained the agreement which had been signed by this government he mentioned production, and only production. He referred to the production of eggs, the production of potatoes, the production of bacon, the production of hogs, the production of ham, the products of the mines, the production of everything-but he did not say a word about distribution. Why? Probably he did not because Mr. Ferguson was here at the time, and Mr. Ferguson spoke to him about honey.
Sir, let us look forward to 1933 when the world conference was held. We know that the conference in 1930 had been a failure, the high tariffs of 1930 and 1931 had proved failures, the conference of 1932 was an utter failure., and then we saw the members of the government going to the world conference. In the midst of the proceedings of that conference we heard that the Prime Minister of Canada had saved it. But he was such a good doctor that only a few days later the conference died of its own weakness. What did my good friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) say when he came back? He

Reform Measures-Mr. Pouliot
said it had been a delightful conference, and that he had made many acquaintances among the representatives of the sixty-three nations who met on that momentous occasion. The world conference meant more. It meant trade with other nations. Canada could not enter into trade with those nations because she was bound by the agreements of 1932. She was gagged and could do nothing because of the Ottawa agreements.
Let us now come to last year. No one need say a word about the world conference, because so far as Canada was concerned nothing was done there. It was another failure. We hear this government boasting about the great benefits derived from the conference of 1932, the Ottawa agreements. Apparently the lion, member for Rosetown (Mr. Loueks) is satisfied with them. Does he know that in the years following that conference our trade with Creat Britain and with other British countries was much less than in the last year the Mackenzie King government held office. Does he know that? I am sure when he entered this house in 1930 he wanted an improvement in trade. I give him the benefit of the doubt and will say that I am sure he was sincere at that time. He repeated, after his leader, that conditions were bad in Canada at that time.

speechtext: We lost our wheat market in 1929, don't forget that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Let me continue. In 1930 did the hon. member not say to the people that conditions were bad in this country? If he did not he was not a faithful follower of his leader who made that statement in every parish, every town and every city of Canada. If they thought conditions were bad in 1930 how is it they think they are so good now when, in fact, they are much worse. Not only that but I would remind the hon. member for Rosetown that statements were made by Tory and U.F.A. speakers advising the wheat growers not to sell their wheat because they would receive much more if they waited and left it in thie pool. He knows it, and he will not deny it. Let me say to my hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Gott) that I am not talking about onions; I am talking about wheat. I say that the state of the wheat market in 1929 was due to the pool of which my hon. friend from Rosetown was a member.

speechtext: Where did you get the information?

speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman is out of order in using that word.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Then I say, in this chamber which is very much alive. What information has the government about farm loans, for instance? The information on that subject is incomplete. I got a little bit of information myself from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics last year about it. I was most interested in the matter, but in a letter signed by the director of that bureau he said: "We cannot certify these figures." And how did they get these figures?? At the time of the census they were asking the farmers what the amount of their debt was. Do you think for a moment that the farmer is going to tell his neighbours or someone in the community the exact amount of his debt? It is absurd. The only way to get at the exact amount of farm mortgages would be to have a careful inspection made in every registry office, with a report based upon that inspection, forwarded to this government through the provincial government. I have frequently asked this government to discuss that matter in the provincial conferences, but I am sure that nothing has ever been done because that information is yet to come. Well, sir, it is all right to be in the clouds, and the Prime Minister is in the clouds. In Halifax, when addressing a gathering of ladies there he said, "My only wish is for eternal salvation." He is in the clouds; he is nearer heaven; but those clouds prevent him from seeing what is going on on earth. He should come to practical facts. Very often, sir, I have asked the hon. gentlemen who surround the Prime Minister to guard against intruders, to prevent all those who are seeking favours from coming into contact with the Prime Minister, all those fellows who are undesirable, so as to give the Prime Minister time to think. Was it done? I am sorry for the Prime Minister and for this country,

Reform Measures-Mr. Pouliot
because his time has been wasted in answering callers who were more importunate than useful from the standpoint of the public good.
And now I have something else to say. One reason why I am most fearful about this legislation is on account of a report which has been made of the speech which was delivered by the right hon. gentleman on Saturday of last week in Montreal. I have here the Montreal Gazette in which it is stated:
The Prime Minister suggested that his talks with Soviet foreign minister Litvinoff at Geneva, and his study of the views of Sir Stafford' Cripps and John Strachey, British radicals, had influenced him to a great extent, while he also pointed out the lessons that could be learned from the French and Russian revolutions.
He is sovie.tizing Canada now, after the failure of the London conference of 1930, the failure of the increase of tariff idea.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
There are some Cossacks there. After the utter failure of the London conference of 1930, the utter failure of the increase in tariffs in 1931, the utter failure of the Ottawa agreements, the utter failure of the world conference and of every policy which has been submitted to us. by the government, this is what we find, as reported in that paper.
Well, sir, I am sorry for this government. They have been talking so much about the alliance that exists between Liberals and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. Do they not now feel ashamed of themselves? Take the speeches which have been delivered in the province of Quebec by the Quebec ministers; are they not ashamed of themselves for being so much congratulated upon their policies by the leaders of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation? It is the vengeance of the Liberal party. We heard our friend the Solicitor General, we heard the Postmaster General, and we heard the Minister of Marine, in the province of Quebec, saying, "Look at the Liberals. The Liberal party does not exist any longer. We have the C.C.F. and the Tory party, those two great parties which enjoy the confidence of the people of Canada." Well, sir, who won the last by-elections throughout Canada, in each province of the dominion? Who won the provincial elections in Ontario, in Nova Scotia and in the west, in Saskatchewan and British Columbia? Who will win every election? Those who will say, "We are strongly opposed to the federal government which is now in power. We must defeat them." This was
said by my noble, generous and capable friend, Mr. Hepburn, in the last provincial election.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I hear hon. gentlemen laughing, but Mr. Hepburn has been pronounced a great son of the province of Ontario, one whom every father and mother would like to have as a son. I see the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott). Does he not know that the four Hepburn candidates in Essex county, with whom I was standing on the platform in Windsor last year, and the other Hepburn candidates as well were elected? The people of Ontario have seen the light. They knew that this man was true to his principles, that he was a true disciple of Mackenzie King; and when he was in this house he was not afraid, any more than I am myself, to speak the language of truth, which is really the language of friendship, to the Prime Minister and his colleagues. That man was earnest; he was sincere; he was true to his convictions and fulfilled his promises-a thing this government has never done. It was because of his sincerity that he had such a wonderful victory in Ontario, and I say to hon. gentlemen to your right, Mr. Speaker, that they should be proud to see a young man of thirty-eight, if not enjoying their own confidence, at any rate enjoying the confidence of the great majority of the people of his native province, so much so that even in the province of Quebec he is just as popular as he is in any other province of confederation.
I have something very nice to read to this house. It is an excerpt from a speech which was delivered by the then leader of the opposition on June 25, 1930, at Cobourg, Ontario:
"Anybody could devise a policy for to-day," the opposition leader declared, "to catch votes, but it is our duty, the duty of statesmen-
This is most humble, most modest.
-to see beyond the horizon."
Is it not delightful, Mr. Speaker? Now, coming to social insurance, it will have to be paid for, and though I cannot quote the exact page of Hansard, I remember distinctly hearing the Prime Minister state in this house that he would accept nothing but a contributory system. Well, how many people do we meet in Ottawa who have not 10 cents with which to buy a sandwich, and how can they pay towards a contributory system of insurance? If this insurance is to solve unemployment, where will the funds come from? Is it true
270	COMMONS
Reform, Measxvres-Mr. Pouliot
that incomes will be severely taxed above $5,000, to the exent of one-third? People have not the money with which to pay-much less than in 1930. Last year in the Gazette of February 9, 1934, I read a report of a speech delivered by the Prime Minister in the Mount Royal hotel, in Montreal, on Realties-not realty. What did he say? The heading is:
Credit of Canada has reached limit premier declares.
People must face fact, Bennett says, and work for future.
Always for the future. He is ashamed of his past; I mean as Prime Minister, otherwise he is a very nice gentleman.
Default impossible.
Dominion must retain place among nations, Canadian club is told-railway problem discussed.
Here I have something delightful. He spoke about the debt of Canada approximating $3,000,000,000. He said:
This was the sum on which Canada had directly to pay interest. Then there were the sums of money which the dominion had guaranteed.
This is in a Tory paper which had found the policy of the government so bad that it had to repudiate it this year.
"That mere statement," the Premier continued, "is enough to make men thoughtful. Put yourself in my place and wonder where the money is coming from to pay the interest. That is the problem we have to think of. And all the theories in the world, my friends-
He did not then say " men and women."
[DOT]-will not solve the problem. It is an actuality, a reality."
All the theories about that so-called reform legislation which is not ready and which, when ready, it is impossible to digest, are not a reality. We have to face a reality. A tremendous debt is bearing down upon the Canadian people and it has to be met. It is hard to meet it because the government has closed this country to the markets of the world. Now it comes with views as to the future just the same as we have already had in the past. Do hon. members remember that when Our Lord had fasted for forty days He was brought to a high mountain and the devil said to him; Kneel before me and all these prosperous cities, all these fertile plains that you see will be yours.	The
answer of Our Lord to Satan was: "Vade Retro Satanas."	" Get thee behind me,
Satan." This is the answer that this government will get from the Canadian people at the next election.

towards the French speaking members of this house as his colleague was last year. We were told over the radio by the Solicitor General that every publication, including Hansard and all others, would appear at the same time in French and English. Here is a most important matter, supply, and we have no French translation, so I do not see why the Minister of Finance should insist on going on. We were told that with the organization of the bureau for translations everything would be fine and all publications would come out simultaneously in both French and English, as from a slot machine. Now we have to wait for the translation of the estimates.
As a French speaking member I insist that we follow the precedent established last year by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals. What he did was well done, and I hope the Minister of Finance will follow the same line. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is here; the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve), the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau), the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) and the right hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), all ministers from the province of Quebec, are here also, and I appeal to them, as representing French speaking people, to tell the Minister of Finance that this discussion should be postponed until the French version of the estimates is tabled. I ask you, sir, to give a ruling on the matter and to decide whether or not we should continue the discussion of supply when we have not the French translation of the estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

speechtext:
As one who took a very active part in connection with the translation bill last year I think it only fair that I should say a word about the lack of the French translation. Repeatedly the Secretary of State and the French ministers made the boast that the amalgamation of the translation bureaux was a step in the right direction and that all documents and reports would be published concurrently in the French and English languages. One of the most vital duties we are called upon to perform in this house is the voting of supply; one of the most important documents to be submitted is the estimates, yet at the very first opportunity we find that the estimates are not available in both languages.
This is a most serious and anomalous situation. We have the remarkable situation that after the promises of the Secretary of State and of the other ministers from Quebec, supported by the French speaking members from that province who sit on the government benches, that this step -would put the French language on a par with the English language.

Supply-Justice

yet at the very first opportunity, and in connection with the most important document to be presented to the house, we are furnished with the English version only. What I stated at the time the bill was under discussion has come true. This bill was a farce. It has achieved only one thing, namely, it has necessitated the translators working unearthly and unholy hours under conditions absolutely foreign heretofore. The results are just what we predicted, namely that the change would lead to confusion. I am not prepared to take my seat without expressing the strongest possible protest. I do not speak with hostility. But I have said what I had to say more particularly in view of the promises made last year by the Secretary of State and lately of the declarations made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) in Montreal that concurrently all documents would be published, translated and deposited on the table of the house.
I believe we should be told why we have not received the estimates printed in French. I have had my English copy of the estimates for five or six days, and I have awaited this opportunity to make these observations. We now have tangible proof of the accuracy of our statement of last year to the effect that the change in translating services would amount to a huge farce. I am protesting as strongly as is within my power against the lack of expedition in publishing the French version.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

speechtext:
The criticisms levelled at the bureau for translations are not well taken. For the first time I think in the history of this parliament, at least for many years, the departmental reports for the past year were laid upon the table of the bouse printed in the French language in the first days of the session. Provision is being made for the very early translation of Hansard reports from English into French. Of course, the official report of Hansard is reported in English and French, but we have made special efforts towards publishing the French translation of the official report on the same day as the official report appears, only a few hours later.
Concerning the translation of the estimates may I say that the bureau proceeded with the translation as soon as the copy was received by the department. I do not know why there was a delay, or even if there was a delay in sending the estimates from the Department of Finance to the translations bureau. However the document has been translated and is now in print. The official proofs of the print were sent to-day from the translations bureau to the Department of Public Printing and

Stationery. The printing has not yet been completed although the composition is complete. The French translation will certainly be ready to-morrow.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

speechtext:
I am prepared to accept the minister's explanation, but it just goes to show that I was right. I did not level my criticism against the staff of translators, as the minister must know. I must say however that the minister is and has in the past been ever prone to accept responsibility for anything done in his department. He has shouldered the responsibility. I am not levelling these criticisms at -the translators, but I have levelled them at the administration and particularly at those members who are responsible for the administration of the law in question. Last year Hansard was published just as it is published to-day. We had Hansard early in the morning, and we still have Hansard early in the morning. Previously however the translators did not have to work the unholy hours they now rmist work. They did not have to begin work at eleven o'clock at night and wait until one o'clock in the morning before they could get copy. At that time they did not have to wait until daylight before they could go home, as they do now. These people are working under conditions which may require the application of legislation concerning working hours. Probably we will have to ask that such legislation may be adapted to translators and other civil servants, if the administration is going to continue to administer affairs as it is now doing.
That is the reason I direct my criticism against the administration. Last year we had no trouble, and in the years past we had no trouble. There was no difficulty until the Secretary of State, moved by some motive, turned the whole department into chaos, and turned the whole thing into turmoil by trying to put in a new system, a sort of reform and something new. Now we find that after all these changes conditions are much worse than they were before.

were willing to receive and accept the French translation four or five days after the official record in English and French was published. speechtext:
I cannot leave it at that, Mr. Chairman. When I gave a question to the assistant clerk of the house as I had done for years past, and the translation, and not only the translation but the question itself as transcribed, and published in the order paper, were wrong, naturally I complained about it. I did not complain about the bureau for translations; I mentioned only one translator. So my hon. friend the Secretary of State is wrong in both instances. He has only to look at the first page of yesterday's Hansard to see what I said. I did not mention the bureau, but one translator. So why should we discuss it further?
What we are discussing is the fact that the estimates are not tabled in French. Whether the French translation is at the bureau or in the Belgian Congo I do not care. The fact is we have not got it in this House of Commons, and as we have not got it here at this very moment, I do not see how the Prime Minister and his colleagues can ask us to consider these estimates. The Prime Minister's colleague who sits to his left, the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) is no longer in the chamber. He should be here when we are discussing this important matter. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to establish an employment and social insurance commission; to provide for a national employment service; for insurance against unemployment; for aid to unemployed persons, and for other forms of social insurance and security, and for purposes related thereto; and to provide for such contributions as may be necessary to carry into effect the proposed legislation.
He said:	I do not know, Mr. Speaker,
whether it would best suit the convenience of hon. gentlemen to consider at the moment the matters that are referred to in the resolution while you are still in the chair, and when questions cannot be asked and answered, or whether it is advisable that you should now leave the chair and the committee be formed at once, so that discussion upon the resolution can take place and I can make a statement and answer questions put to me. I am entirely in the hands of the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I think it would expedite matters if Your Honour were to leave the chair and we got into committee immediately.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I do not intend to enter into a discussion at any length with respect to the general subject of unemployment insurance; I will do that when the opportunity is afforded under the rules for the introduction of a bill founded on the resolution. The resolution contemplates a bill being submitted to the chamber dealing with the matters that are mentioned in the resolution itself. Sometimes the custom has been followed of discussing upon the resolution the details of a measure founded thereupon. Such I believe is unsound practice.
Unemployment Insurance

First of all, the resolution seeks the introduction of a bill to establish an employment and social insurance commission. It is proposed that an unemployment insurance measure shall be introduced, founded upon this resolution, and before I go further I should like to point out that on April 29, 1931, in this chamber, I made this statement:
I propose, if we are spared as a government and as individuals, that the information we will have before our term of office is ended shall be crystallized into the form of legislative proposals to be submitted to this house. I have never had any illusions as to what is involved; I have none now. I have never had any desire other than that the legislation placed upon the statute book, whether by this government or by some other, shall be legislation based upon knowledge, and not upon mere guesswork.
The next year I made the same observation. I endeavoured to explain on that occasion that any unemployment measure, called an insurance measure, must necessarily imply some understanding of the risk that is incurred by the insurers. That seemed to me to be elementary. The difficulty had been that the census returns, although the report had been made, had not been analyzed for the purpose of ascertaining just what they disclosed with respect to unemployment. I mentioned the other day just what the returns did show as to the numbers of unemployed! on the first of June. Now I will not do more than recall what I said in 1931 as to the factors that must be considered and the elements that enter into the preparation of an unemployment insurance measure.
This bill contemplates administration by a commission and an effort will be made by the measure to see that it is freed as far as may be from political control. One of the difficulties in all countries where legislation dealing with unemployment insurance has been introduced has been that the political element has entered into discussions and in a large sense, in more than one country, has frustrated the values attaching to such legislation. It will be observed further that the legislation which will be introduced on this bill, which introduction I shall move when this resolution has been adopted, contemplates the creation of a commission for the purpose of dealing with this matter.
Then the resolution says:
To provide for a national employment .service.
I shall not now follow in detail the various laws that were passed in Great Britain to deal with unemployment insurance beginning in 1911; nor shall I deal with the reports made by commissions that from time to time have considered the matter and determined
fMr. Bennett.]
whether there should be an extension of benefits, an increase in premiums; nor shall I at the moment consider those who are eligible because a resolution does not contemplate that discussion being had before the measure itself is introduced. But I shall say this, that in Great Britain the very foundation of the effort was found in the national employment service. That is, the labour offices, or as we call them in Canada, the employment offices, may transfer labour from one point to another, and provided there is unemployment at one point and requirements at another the labour may be transferred from the point where there is a surplus to the point where it may be utilized. In this country as is known, consequent upon the treaty of peace and the conferences that were held, the setting up of the international labour office, we did provide for the institution in Canada of employment offices. The dominion became a party to those offices being established and in a large sense provides for their maintenance. Those offices have an important part to play in the legislation which will be submitted to the house, an important part to play for the pin-pose of providing information to the commission constantly as to where there is a surplus of labour, for instance, in a single province where there is a surplus at one point and requirements at another, and the principles that were adopted in Great Britain have been the principles largely followed so far as possible having regard to our area in this country.
Then it will be observed that we are providing for insurance against unemployment. Insurance in essence is an indemnity. Obviously it will be impossible to provide for insurance that will be a complete indemnity with respect to unemployment. There must be first of all the determination of the probable numbers that will be affected. We have taken terms of years; the statistical department has determined what the average would be and from that we have endeavoured to select just what would be the likely number of unemployed in any one year having regard to the average numbers employed during the period to which I have referred, namely, ten or eleven years. Upon that of course, must be determined the premium that should be paid. That is an actuarial computation depending naturally upon the benefits that are to be conferred when the insurance becomes a claim. As regards the part of the resolution providing for unemployment insurance, I shall not go into detail now more than to say that the premium shall be paid by the employer, the worker

Unemployment Insurance
and the state, the state's contribution being the cost largely of administration, and when the bill is introduced I shall give the history of other countries in that regard. That, however, is how the premium is to be paid. The amount of premium of course will vary with the ages of the insured; it will vary also with the averages of unemployment and employment as shown from the figures which we have obtained from the statistical department and upon which the actuaries have exercised their talents.
That being determined, the next question is a very simple one: What benefits are to be secured from the premium thus paid? Obviously the benefits as in most insurance of that kind issued by private enterprises and companies, are limited as to the period of time during which they will be paid. Sometimes health insurance provides for benefits for thirteen weeks, sometimes for twenty-six weeks, sometimes for a longer period depending upon the amount of premium paid and what the actuarial figures indicate as to the character and nature of the risk. In this instance I shall indicate to the house when I introduce the bill the history of other countries in that regard. At this time for purposes of the resolution it is only necessary to point out that we contemplate the maintenance of those features which differentiate insurance from any other form of contract. There is the payment of a premium by the workman, his employer and the state; those three together are responsible for the premium which is received by the commissioners and which is administered in the way of benefits depending on claims being made by those who come within the terms of the statutory requirements, namely finding themselves unemployed under the conditions that are mentioned in the bill. That of course is a matter to be determined with great care. Whether the period shall be thirteen weeks or fourteen weeks, what number of claims may be made by a workman within a given period of time, what must be his necessary contribution as a minimum before he can make a claim, how his contributions shall accumulate during a given time-all these matters have been considered in all the European countries and we have obtained the benefit of their experience. When I introduce the bill I shall make known to the house what that experience shows so that it may be available on Hansard for hon. members.
After having provided for benefits of that kind, the resolution states:
For aid' to unemployed persons, and for other forms of social insurance and security.
We merely provide for the amplification of that in cases where for exceptional reasons a workman has preferred no claim for a long period of time, say five, six, or seven years, where he has worked continuously, he might then secure larger benefits than he would otherwise be entitled to on the strict construction of his statutory policy or right to claim. That is a very simple matter depending of course upon whether he has been able to maintain his work from day to day and from month to month for a long period of time.
The next point deals with the problem of the payment of the necessary premiums, that is such contributions as may be necessary to carry into effect the proposed legislation. I do not of course consider that on a resolution I am within the rules of the house in endeavouring to discuss what have been described as constitutional questions, but I think I may anticipate what I propose to say on the introduction of the bill by pointing out to the house that I have no doubt whatever as to the constitutionality of the bill which will be submitted to parliament. I have no doubt at all that it is within our legislative powers. Whatever doubts may have arisen in times past-and I confess that I was one of those who had grave doubts as to our constitutional powers with respect to a matter of this kind-I think it is fair to say that there are two reasons why those doubts in my mind have been entirely dissipated, and I trust they are reasons which will be sufficiently strong to commend themselves to the sympathetic consideration and I think approval of every member of this chamber.
In the first place it will be recalled that we entered into a treaty of peace as part of the British empire. It will be recalled that in 1919 Canada executed the peace treaty as a part of the British empire. This parliament ratified that treaty by the Treaties of Peace Act of 1919, and not only in the covenant of the League of Nations but also in one of the articles of the treaty itself express provision is made for matters dealing with questions of labour. It will also be recalled that pursuant to the powers thereby conferred there was called together a great labour conference which met at Washington the very same year when the late Senator Robertson was Minister of Labour, Mr. Rowell, then President of the Council, was Acting Minister of External Affairs, and the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition was one of the advisers who attended as a former minister of labour. That conference determined that certain acts
Unemployment Insurance

were advisable and that a certain course of conduct should be pursued with respect to labour. I will do no more at present than say that conventions have from that time been drawn up, the various nations of the world have indicated their approval of them, and Canada, although approving of them, has availed herself of that provision of the peace treaty which said with respect to federal communities that if they did not desire to deal with these matters they might instead recommend them to the provinces. Recommendations have from time to time been made by the government of the day to the provinces. But I know of no reason why parliament should not exercise its' power under section 132 of the British North America Act and deal as a part of the British empire with the obligations which we accepted and which are created under the peace treaty and by subsequent conferences. Many ratifications have taken place by this parliament of conventions arrived at, and ratifications will be sought with respect to other matters that have to do with social problems and social legislation.
There is another reason which is wider still than that in the narrow constitutional sense. Since we first began to consider these matters there has been, as has been pointed out, a widening conception of the power of the federal authority with respect to many matters. In the aviation case, for instance, it was held that the federal power had exclusive jurisdiction to deal with matters pertaining to the use of the air. In the radio case a similar decision was reached. Therefore we have in the terms of the judgment of the court of last resort a statement in both cases of a widening sense of the power of the central authority, and when those two are coupled with the additional powers that have to do with interprovincial and international trade, peace, order and good government, and the power of taxation for the purpose of making contributions to such a fund, the law officers of the crown have no doubt, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) is clear, that in the light of the decisions as we now have them the legislation in the terms in which it will be offered to this house is within the competence of this parliament.
I do not think I shall make any more detailed statement on this resolution. I realize that on the introduction of the bill founded upon it I shall be expected to make a more elaborate statement as to the conditions in other countries, as to the history of such legislation, especially, in Great Britain, whose fMr. Bennett.]
act we have largely copied, and the effort that has been made, shall I say, to adapt the legislation of Great Britain to the conditions of this country.

speechtext: To answer that question at the moment would involve dealing with a mass of detail. It will depend upon the number of payments made by an assured within a given period of time. If for instance an assured should make the required number of payments, as provided in the English act, within a year, his right to claim would arise immediately thereafter. The whole theory upon which such legislation is based in other countries-in Great Britain, for instance, whose legislation we have followed, is that within a given time the worker makes a given number of contributions and thereby obtains the right to make a claim. His premium earns him the right to make a claim if he is validly unemployed. If he is not unemployed he is laying up for himself treasure in the future with regard to what may be called supplementary benefits that accrue under the statute.
