subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Of course the governments that enacted the Lemieux act, the Board of Commerce Act and the various insurance acts were satisfied that those acts were within the competence of this parliament. But unfortunately their validity was challenged by the provinces, and victoriously Does not the right hon. gentleman think that it would be better to try to come to an agreement and understanding on the matter prior to enactment than to take the chance of having the act declared unconstitutional by the court?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I can quite appreciate the point made by the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). The fact is that the Lemieux act was generally regarded by lawyers who were fairly well informed as being unsound constitutionally in view not of decisions of the moment but, I think, a decision subsequent to the date of its enactment in which, under the late Lord Haldane, there had been placed upon provincial powers an interpretation somewhat widening them from the conception which obtained at the time the Lemieux act was passed. With respect to the insurance acts it will foe recalled that, commencing with the Citizens' Insurance Company and Parsons, the privy council decided that statutory conditions could be imposed by provincial legislatures upon policies issued by companies licensed by the federal power. From that decision there followed a long train of decisions terminating in the insurance reference and the various cases that arose subsequent to that by reason of legislation enacted by this parliament as well as by the provinces.
Probably it is within the hon. gentleman's memory that the Lemieux act was not attacked until some twenty years after it had been enacted, if my memory serves me aright, while in the Board of Commerce case the attack was immediate and successful. It was not, I think, until the case brought by Snyder had been dealt with that the Lemieux act was finally dealt with.
Unemployment Insurance

We have not the slightest doubt at the moment, and unless the hon. gentleman is able to throw some doubt on it that we have not at the present time we can see no escape from our having jurisdinction, for the simple and obvious reason that section 132 of the British North America Act provides:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
Those words were considered in the aviation and radio cases, and the construction placed upon them is now a matter of record. Therefore, having regard to what has taken place under the peace treaty and having regard to the position taken by this parliament, I do not think there is any doubt as to our position.
As to the second question, with regard to the desirability of discussing the matter with the provinces, when we did discuss this matter the attitude taken by some of the provinces was one of great relief to think that the dominion would undertake a national obligation of this character. Some provinces, however, took the view that this was an interference with their exclusive powers. They said, "We do not desire to discuss the question of the merits of the legislation, for the jurisdiction is either exclusive to us or it is exclusive to the federal power," or in other words to parliament. The question of the obligation under the treaty section so far as I know has not been doubted by any province in the confederation, and if it is not necessary to amend the constitution to effectuate the purpose we have in mind I do not think any good purpose is to be served by doing so. It will be recalled that when this government came into office neither the aviation nor the radio case had been decided. I think perhaps hon. members will remember the observation of a great jurist that the expansion of law by judicial interpretation, even when applied to a modern statute, is that modern conditions may be met even though the statute is of long standing or great age, and the privy council has seen fit to put upon our constitution a somewhat wider interpretation, when dealing with aviation and radio. I think the hon. gentleman will particularly recall the radio case-

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: And that is the way in which women became persons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
That is another case, and I thank my hon. friend for reminding me of it, although truthfully I never had any doubt

about it myself; I never doubted that the decision would be as it was. The Minister of Justice, together with his entire staff and the law officers of the crown, have given the matter much attention and they are clear that at the moment, unless there is some curtailment of federal power by decisions that may arise hereafter, which I think is not likely, this legislation is within our competence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The Prime
Minister has stated that this is to be a contributory scheme, with contributions by the federal authorities, the provinces and the employees.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Not by the provinces;
by the employers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Are the contributions under this act to be voluntary or compulsory?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
These, of course, are
compulsory.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Are any
classes of the community specifically excluded from the provisions of the legislation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Yes. I might say to
the right hon. gentleman that this was one of the matters I proposed to deal with on the introduction of the bill. He, as an old countryman, will recall that under the report of one of the commissions both the banking and insurance fraternities entirely exclude themselves from the operations of the act. The same principle runs through this proposed legislation.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I understand that there is no contribution by the provincial authority or government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: There is none confemplated by the bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I should like to ask if, included in the unemployment insurance act, there will be also measures dealing with sickness' and invalidity insurance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
That is not dealt with
in the way of conferring benefits; that is dealt with in a very limited sense, in the view that matters both of relief and of health necessarily must be within the provincial rather than the federal jurisdiction.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Then do I understand that
these are not to form part of the legislation dealing with unemployment insurance?

Unemployment Insurance

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
They are dealt with in
part, but as I say not in the sense of conferring benefits under it for the premiums paid, except in so far as .they may constitute the basis of unemployment, if that is what the hon. gentleman means.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
No, I have in mind the
British act, under which benefits are paid to those who are sick or who suffer from invalidity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Where unemployment
follows as the result of the conditions mentioned in the statute, without going into them in detail, the benefits are payable, of course, but there is no system of what you call health insurance such as you have in private enterprise; there is no method by wdiich policies may be secured such as may be had for accident and ill health. That is distinguished from unemployment. The basis of the premium, and the basis of the scheme, is unemployment.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The
Prime Minister knows that under the British act the same statute contains provisions dealing with national health insurance.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Would that be compulsory
insurance?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Is there any provision in this bill for the men now unemployed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Not in so far as it is
relief.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Is there any supplemental measure in connection with the bill by which those now unemployed will be cared for?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Not under this bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Then it seems to
me quite obvious that this measure will be of very limited application.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That is a hope.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
No, the point is
that if the bill is based on the earnings of the workmen, and if only upon those earnings he can base any claim upon the fund, I think it is obvious that there is no provision whatever for the half million people who are now unemployed, involving over a million individuals now in receipt of relief. There would seem to be no provision whatever for this great class of people, including those who are now in receipt of relief in their own homes,
those who are housed in the various refuges in the cities and those who are in relief camps of various kinds. I think it ought to be made Very clear that there is nothing whatever in this bill to provide for the outstanding evils of the depression, which we now face. Further than that, when the Prime Minister speaks of the claims as being based on actuarial experience his observations would mean that for only a few' weeks after a man became unemployed could he draw any unemployed benefits. That may be all very w'ell in normal times, but under the circumstances prevailing to-day it would mean that after a very few weeks indeed a man would be no better off than he was before. His claim would be exhausted.
I understand that contributions are to be obligatory. Undoubtedly that will mean that those who are receiving very low wages-and the price spreads commission has revealed that a great many of our people are in that position-will have their present low wages still further reduced, which will work an extreme hardship upon them and means privation to their wives and children. They are not now receiving a living wage, and the contribution here involved would mean a still further diminution of the small amount they are now receiving. That I believe must be a very serious consideration.
I understand any commission set up is to be so constituted that employers and employees will be represented thereon. We are informed, however, that it will be removed from political control. That may be all very well in the case of railways, where only money is concerned, but I believe it is a more serious consideration when we are dealing with human beings. For instance we are told that administration of the new plan will to a large extent rest upon unemployment offices, and that it may be possible to shift people from one particular point to another. Does that mean that a commission quite removed from political control will have power to shift people from northern Ontario down to Quebec or from Manitoba out to Vancouver, and to insist that those people move whether they like it or not? That to my mind is an important question for consideration.
The Prime Minister has referred to the experience of European countries. The experience of European countries during the depression has been that unemployment schemes have failed to function. That is true in England, where supplementary to the regular unemployment insurance scheme they
Unemployment Insurance

have had to adopt relief measures commonly known as the dole. I had hoped that in the proposed bill we would find some supplementary provisions which would at least bring us in line with the provision in Great Britain. Apparently, however, there is to be nothing of that kind. The unemployment insurance scheme was originated in Germany some years ago and was carried on in that country very systematically. We recall, however, that as soon as the full force of the depression struck Germany the scheme broke down, simply because, based as it was on the earnings and contributions of the workers, the amounts paid were reduced as also the time during which benefits were paid. The scheme failed to provide for their needs in an emergency.
I welcome the strong stand taken by the government that constitutionally they have the right to do something in this matter. Some of us have pleaded for that for a long time. We have said that if Canada had the right to enter into a treaty she had the right to carry out its terms. I am very glad the government has taken that position, and I hope they will see the matter through. However, when we come to meeting the pressing unemployment situation we are facing to-day I think we must confess that the Prime Minister's statement is most unsatisfactory and most disappointing. It makes no provision for meeting the claims and needs of a vast number of our fellow citizens who for some ten years past have been suffering.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: What would the hon. member suggest as the proper way to draft the legislation?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
As I have said I
agree with the legislation as far as it goes, but I submit that it helps only a very limited number of people.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: How is the hon. member going to help those people?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
That is not a
matter to be discussed here. I can quite readily go into it, and shall take an early opportunity to do so. All I want to do on this occasion is to make some general observations and not to go into the matter in great detail. We have not yet the measure before us, but I do think that on the statement made by the Prime Minister it is proper immediately to recognize that, however admirable some provisions in the plan may be, it does not meet the needs of the great mass of the unemployed, and that a

considerable time will be required to build up a reserve sufficient to be of much service even to those now at work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I greatly regret that the hon. member has seen fit to confuse relief and unemployment insurance. There could be no such thing as a provision for voluntary relief or relief being given to those who are not insured. No actuary would talk about a program for insurance if he had no data upon which to formulate his figures or calculations. Relief is one thing; insurance is another. Unemployment insurance contemplates just what it says, namely the payment of benefits dependent as to their amount upon the extent of the premium payments made by the worker, the employer and the state.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That was not the experience in Great Britain when they attempted to extend their unemployment scheme.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
In England you have a unitary system of government. That has been said so often that I repeat it simply because the hon. member is well aware of it. I fear this parliament has no jurisdiction over direct relief in that sense, nor has the treaty anything to do with it, nor have the other provisions of the British North America Act anything to do with it. We are now dealing with a national matter in which we provide that if a worker pays three and a half cents a day, if a like sum is paid by the employer and the state makes a contribution necessary to administer the system-amounting we will say to something slightly less than the amount I have stated or possibly slightly more-the worker secures the benefits because of payments made. The actuarial computations are made upon that basis.
Relief is an entirely different matter, and depends on entirely different circumstances. It cannot be the subject matter of actuarial computations. There is not the scientific data upon which to predicate any degree of assistance. As a result of discussions and conferences between those who have the primary responsibility and this government-or this parliament, I should say-contributions in aid are made to meet extraordinary circumstances under which those people are living.
There is a fact that the hon. member constantly disregards, although I do not think he does it purposely. There never has been a time in Canada when due to seasonal unemployment there has not been a very large number of unemployed. Estimates vary, but an estimate was made in 1930 at the time my right hon. friend held office as to what would

Unemployment Insurance
be involved under normal conditions. It was learned that there were never less than 150,000 unemployed scattered over the country, after it had reached a population exceeding 10,000,000. There are estimates greatly in excess of that.
In days gone by, before the depression, a workman could accummulate during the summer money sufficient to care for his family during the winter. Some worked only in the winter-or to put it the other way round, worked only in the summer so as to care for their families in the winter. But those reserves have entirely disappeared and been dissipated because there has been no work to enable those workers to accumulate a fresh reserve to deal with the period of unemployment brought about because of the fact that they were seasonal employees. That is the situation that has brought about relief in this country, until that slack can be taken up and employment provided for those who have been seasonally employed, to enable them to provide the reserve to care for themselves and their families as heretofore. It is a problem *which the local community, the city, town, municipality and province are dealing with, with the aid and assistance of grants which have been made to all the provinces in, say, some reasonable proportion to their necessities.
But on the next point, as to the condition of the unemployed, that is a matter which we have discussed every year with the provinces. *Only a few months ago we discussed it with them, and they may or may not desire to discuss it with us again. Presumably they will desire to do so, in which event parliament will be asked to consider what it conceives to be the best way to deal with it, having regard to the suggestions which the provinces make.
I should like once more to remind the house of the fact that in every instance the manner adopted to deal with the unemployment problem in the several provinces was arrived at by representatives of the provinces in consultation with dominion authorities. There was this limitation, that there were differences as to the extent to which they should secure assistance. Some thought that they should receive a larger sum per month than the sum received, but in every instance the method, using that word in the broad sense, was a method which was approved after a conference between the provinces and the dominion.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Does the Prime
Minister suggest that it is beyond the powers of the dominion government to meet a national emergency such as unemployment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I have not any doubt
that with the change, the diminution of unemployment, that has taken place during the last fifteen or eighteen months, it would be very difficult, if you follow the language of Lord Haldane's judgment, to assert jurisdiction on behalf of the dominion.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I wonder if the Prime Minister would explain this point to enlighten my ignorance. I understood him to quote section 132 of the British North America Act as giving this parliament the dominant power to disregard or ignore the claims of jurisdiction put forward by the provinces in dealing with this matter, but when he read that section it seemed to me that it referred entirely to giving the Dominion of Canada dominance in the matter of carrying out obligations in relation to foreign countries only, and did not deal with domestic relations inside Canada as between the dominion and the provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The section in question
mentioned specifically the province, and the interpretation placed upon the section by the privy council was the foundation of my observations. I would suggest to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that it is impossible to deal with the questions he raises adequately until he has seen the bill, and this is not the time at which to read sections. There is not a section before the house until such time as an opportunity has been given to introduce the bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The Prime
Minister has referred to conferences with the provinces and said, if I understood him aright, that whatever was done was done as a result of agreement between the dominion and the provinces. May I ask him, if at one of the conferences, I think two years ago, he did not ask the provinces which of their powers and services they were prepared to surrender? Did he get any answers to that question, and if so, what were the answers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman is quite correct. The answer that I gave to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was an answer with respect to relief, which was the subject matter of discussion and agreement. But as to the question of the surrender of powers with respect to social services and whether the provinces desired to surrender their powers to the dominion, different views were expressed by different provinces. Some of the provinces, without naming them, were rather anxious that that should be done; others were not, and the question as to the terms and conditions that
Unemployment Insurance

some of them might think desirable was vaguely discussed, but no conclusions were arrived at. It was not in any sense upon those discussions that this measure was framed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: There was r.o agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Oh no.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister what is intended by the words " to provide for a national employment service."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Was the hon. gentleman
in the house when I opened my observations?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I pointed out that that was an amplification only of an existing statute that deals with unemployment services, and that it came within the declarations made at the first conference of the International Labour Office after the treaty of peace.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I take it, then, that it is intended to extend the labour employment offices that we have.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: To utilize them for the purposes of this measure and to extend the scope of their activities.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: May I ask what is intended by the words "for aid to unemployed persons?"

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I endeavoured briefly to explain that in this sense: After a man has accumulated a substantial reserve by reason of having made contributions, and has not made a claim for benefits, he might be unemployed for a period that was the maximum provided by the statute; and having regard to the fact that he had not made a claim against the fund there is a provision that would enable him to receive benefits as an unemployed person because of the fact that he did not make a claim against the fund commensurate with the premiums that he had paid.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Then in reality it would not be insurance that he was receiving.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: It is to make that clear.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: But a species of bonus?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Yes. In life and accident companies, as the hon. gentleman is doubtless aware, if you have an accident policy and you have not made any claim against it, as no doubt my hon. friend has not done, every year there is added to the amount of the policy probably ten per cent. In this instance, in order to make it conform to the 
general principles that govern matters of this kind, there has been an attempt to make it plain that there is a clear distinction between the payment of an insurance which resulted from the payment of premiums, and the payment of moneys which have not been exhausted in the payment of benefits that a man has not claimed because of his continuous employment.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: The Prime Minister also says in his resolution: "to provide for other forms of social insurance and security." I take it that the other forms of security are health insurance. But did I understand the Prime Minister to say that we are not going into the health insurance business?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Not in that sense.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Then what is meant by the words "other forms of security?"

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That arises out of the accumulation of funds which have not been utilized-again it is the same thing-for the purpose of payment of claims that might be made for benefits under the fund. The details set forth in the bill seem to me to warrant the use of those words, "other forms of security." It is really another form of security which is not strictly insurance, and it is brought about by reason of the man's own persistence and sound health, his strength and powers of endurance which have freed the fund from claims.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: It is all part of the unemployment insurance?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
It has nothing to do with
any other species of insurance?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Not in that sense.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: The Prime Minister has made it quite clear that this is an insurance scheme and has nothing to do with relief. The man who does not contribute by way of premiums cannot receive any benefits; I think that is quite clear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That is, those who are not employed now or in the future and do not pay premiums will not receive any benefits whatsoever. My colleague behind me says that it is compulsory, that the man must pay; but I say to him that a man who is not employed and has no money cannot be made to pay.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Quite so.

Unemployment Insurance

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I was going to make a reference to the statement that the scheme is both compulsory and contributory. I was going to ask, although possibly this should be asked later on after the bill is introduced, just what method will be employed for enforcing the contributions. Will the contributions be taken direct from the workman, the man who is insured, or will the payments be exacted from his employer? It occurs to me that if you want to be sure that you get contributions you will probably have to take them from the employer. This question might arise: A man might be making his contributions through his employer over a period of time and then become unemployed, and yet he might still be able to make contributions to continue his insurance. Perhaps the Prime Minister might enlarge on that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I can answer one part
of the question at once without going into details. Contributions will be made in the first instance by the employer, as the hon. gentleman has well contemplated, and the methods of attaching stamps to cards, and books, and matters of that kind will be dealt with in the act in detail. The general principle however is as he has mentioned.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Is there any provision whereby, if he is unemployed, his contributions may be collected?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: If he is unemployed he makes a claim against the fund.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
But he might still want to
contribute to increase the reserve.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
It is contemplated that
within a certain number of days he shall make his claim against the fund.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: What is the shortest period before benefits are payable?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
That depends on three
things: first, the number of contributions; secondly, the period of time within which they are made; and thirdly, the number of days of unemployment that will enable him to make the claim. I think we have adopted a compromise of nine days, but I will verify that in the bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
From the remarks made by
the Prime Minister it is obvious that this bill does not begin to touch the fringe of the unemployment situation; in other words, it is a bill that does not deal with unemployment but with those who are employed. It makes provision for those who are employed
at the present time but who on some future occasion may be unemployed and who will therefore receive benefits to which they have subscribed. To what extent that will ultimately ameliorate the unemployment situation it is probably difficult to state at the present time, but one thing ought to be made clear to the house and the country, and particularly to the people who are mostly affected by a measure of this sort; whilst we are engaged in what is termed a reform parliament, to grapple with social problems of an immediate nature, this bill will not, either at this session or at any future session, touch the great problem of unemployment. That must be borne in mind. The impression has gone abroad, to a very large extent from statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite, by the Prime Minister and those closely associated with him-

ministers of the crown make statements to the house they have at least some effect so far as the people of the dominion are concerned, and this legislation has been looked upon as one of the most important items if not the most important item of the government program to be brought forward in the current session. If that is so, I presume that this legislation is intended, or at any rate the impression has gone abroad that it is intended in some way to deal with the problem of unemployment, which I regard as one of the most important problems which parliament has to face. And yet the bill does not touch the fringe of the unemployment situation.
It is quite true, as pointed out by the Prime Minister, that the number of those who are out of work at the present time has considerably diminished in comparison with the number who were out of work a couple of years ago. I remember that in 1932 when I used the figure of 750,000 persons out of work it was scoffed at by members on the government side of the house; they said that we were exaggerating the number out of work.

Unemployment Insurance
Now the Prime Minister tells parliament that the figure has dwindled from 750,000 to approximately 400,000. It might show a tremendous drop, but I have been trying in my own way to ascertain the extent of unemployment in the country, and taking the present period and a year ago I find that the number of people on relief, which is a fairly good criterion of those out of work, has diminished in the large industrial areas approximately ten per cent. In one of the largest cities of Canada I took the matter up with one of the aldermen closely associated with unemployment and he told me that the reason there has been a drop in relief is that those not deserving of relief have been cut off. Having made calculations to-day on the basis of government figures, I come to the conclusion that there must be now approximately 600,000 who are out of work. It is quite true that figures can be both construed and misconstrued, but I venture to assert, in view of relief figures which are so obvious to all of us, that the drop has not been from 750,000 to 400,000, but that there are to-day approximately 600,000 people out of work for whom this employment insurance bill offers not one ray of hope.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was making a few remarks on (Mr. Heaps.]
this question. I dealt with the unemployed in relation to this bill. For a number of years past the organizations of unemployed of this country have been petitioning I presume members of parliament and the government with a view to the establishment of a comprehensive unemployment insurance scheme whereby those who are out of work might be able to receive some benefits from it. Unfortunately the resolution now before us which foreshadows the proposals of the government deals with legislation from which I am afraid the unemployed themselves have very little hope of benefiting.
I can well realize that within the confines of the capitalistic structure it will be next to impossible to create an unemployment insurance scheme that will be actuarially sound and at the same time take within its compass the vast numbers of men and women at present out of work. In other words, if we are to have any unemployment insurance scheme based on an actuarial computation, one that can support itself, it is bound to have a very restricted number of unemployed within its orbit. If I remember correctly-and I stand subject to correction because I am speaking now from memory-when the unemployment insurance scheme was first introduced in Great Britain, as was pointed out this afternoon by the Prime Minister, the average number of unemployed computed for was round about five per cent. Since then, as a result of the ingenuity of man and the introduction of modern machinery into the modes of production, unemployment has naturally tended to increase to a very large extent, making it more difficult to have any unemployment insurance scheme which will give all those who are unemployed and cannot be employed in industry the benefits of such a measure. Consequently in Great Britain after the war, probably when large numbers were out of work, their scheme became actuarially unsound and vast sums of money had to be transferred from the national exchequer to the unemployment insurance fund to keep it solvent. I do not know if even at this date these sums have been returned from the unemployment insurance fund to the imperial exchequer. So to-day when we are attempting to deal with this scheme of unemployment insurance, if it is going to be sound actuarially as is apparently the intention in the bill to be founded on the resolution, it cannot take into consideration the vast numbers of people who are at present unfortunately out of work.

speechtext:
It no doubt relates to the measure we are now discussing; that is, the question of unemployment insurance is the most important, or one of the most important of the reform measures which the government have to present to this house at this session of parliament. If that be the case, then this is to be one of the measures the government intends to bring to the attention of parliament in order to deal with the pressing problems that now confront us. I claim that in so far as it is going to affect the vast numbers of men and women who are at present out of work it will have very little effect upon their status. I am anxious to see the government implement not exactly the promise but the impression that was created upon the minds of the people of this country by the speeches made by the Prime Minister.
For a number of years I have advocated in this house a scheme of unemployment insurance, and when the Prime Minister pointed out this afternoon that in 1931 a resolution on this subject was introduced in this house, it was my resolution and at that time the Prime Minister gave a pledge that during the lifetime of this parliament he would introduce legislation dealing with unemployment insurance. It is apparent that any scheme of unemployment insurance at this time does not deal fundamentally with unemployment, and I am extremely anxious that the government should undertake at this session of parliament such reform measures as will have a lasting effect upon the economic life of this country. As far as this measure is concerned all it will have the effect of doing is to create some scheme of social insurance whereby the employer, the employee and the state will all contribute to a scheme, and when people are entitled to benefits on an actuarial basis they will receive in the form of benefits about the same amount of money they now receive when they are on direct relief or the dole. I prefer this unemployment insurance scheme to the granting of direct relief, the dole as commonly called, but I point out as strongly as I can that the bill as outlined this afternoon fails to deal fundamentally with the

unemployment situation, and I am anxiously looking forward to the other legislation which the government have in contemplation on the question of hours of work, minimum pay and so on, which I regard as far more important legislation than that introduced this afternoon.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I should like to discuss this question from a slightly different angle from that followed thus far. The Prime Minister has introduced this as part of his social legislation, and it has been received with acclaim in many part of the country. However I cannot but think that many people have given little consideration to the measure and to its possible effects upon various classes of the community. It has already been pointed out that so far as meeting immediate needs is concerned this measure is utterly inadequate. That is, it cannot be considered as emergency legislation. Legislation of this kind would better be introduced in times of prosperity than in times of depression. It is in the seven fat years that we have to lay up for the seven lean years. Where the blame lies for not having done this sooner I shall not discuss at the moment.
The Prime Minister has said that this legislation is based upon the English act. I think it can be asserted without fear of contradiction that to establish an unemployment insurance act in England was much simpler than to do so in Canada. In England to a much greater extent than in Canada men are tied to a particular occupation and a particular section of the country. It is true that in Canada we have a few industries to which this measure would be of easy application, for example the railroads. When men enter railway service it is generally with the expectation of making it their life work. The same might be true of large industrial institutions, and perhaps of large mercantile institutions. But there is a great mass of smaller businesses to which it seems to me it will be impossible for legislation of this kind to apply. Then to a much greater extent than in England our population is transient; men are in Halifax to-day and in Vancouver tomorrow.

speechtext: Well, not quite so soon.

speechtext:
An aeroplane would do it; but let us say some intermediate point. The point is that men are not tied to a particular occupation or to a particular locality. With regard to this large number of transients it seems to me that there will be great difficulty in giving them any practical benefit from this scheme.

Whatever I say in criticism of this legislation, I do not wish to seem to be lacking in sympathy for people who through no fault of their own are unemployed. A large number of people who under normal conditions would be earning good wages have through no fault of theirs been forced to accept relief. We must of necessity have pity for people in that position. Then we cannot but think of the tragic position in which the rising generation find themselves, young men and young women growing up having never learned to work, through lack of opportunity. The effect is indeed deplorable.
While I do not wish to seem to offer opposition to the principle of this proposed legislation, yet I think it is necessary for us to consider the matter from some aspects that have not hitherto been considered. The effects of the bill will reach far beyond the people immediately affected, and it is to some of these possible effects that I wish to draw attention. The intention of course is to provide against temporary unemployment. It seems to me it will affect people according to how they are constituted. Legislation of this kind is likely to be a savour of life unto life and of death unto death. There are large numbers of people to-day on relief who feel humiliated by accepting that relief, who feel that it is beneath their dignity, although they are forced to accept it. There was a tragic illustration of this in Winnipeg a short time ago where it was reported that a woman, having been taunted with being on relief, killed her two children and committed suicide. I am happy to believe that there are large numbers of people who, given temporary relief as provided by this bill, would under normal conditions make good and suffer no deterioration from receiving the benefits provided. On the other hand we are compelled to admit that there is another class, and I regret to say that the number is increasing, who are beginning to say that society owes them a living and are determined to get it whether they render any service or not. True, in these times we cannot apply rigidly the principle that if a man will not work neither shall he eat, though that is a very good maxim in normal times. But I regret to say that the number of those who are willing to live upon the community is increasing; we have abundant evidence of it. A very striking article appeared in a recent issue of the Atlantic Monthly, by Newton Baker, entitled The Decay of Self-Reliance. He gave many illustrations of the effect the present depression is having upon people, such as that of a man and his wife who said they were going to the Chicago fair and then going on relief. He

Unemployment Insurance
stated, and it is undoubtedly true, that one of the effects of the English legislation had been to cause men to debate with themselves whether it was better to take the wages offered them or to accept the dole. I am afraid this legislation will to a very large extent increase the number of people who take that attitude towards life.
I realize the difficult circumstances in which we are placed; I realize that the times through which we are passing call for measures we would not think of adopting in normal times, although as I have said a measure of this kind would be better brought forward when conditions were normal rather than in a time of depression. But this legislation is going to have another effect on another class of people; I refer to the taxpayers, wherever they are. The employer who is to contribute to this fund will add the amount of his contribution to the price of his goods, whatever they may be. To a large extent unionized labour may be able to shift the burden also, but the class of people whom I represent, the great agricultural community, never can shift the burden on to anyone. They have to bear it. The effect of this legislation and of all legislation of this nature will be simply to increase the burden placed upon the farmer. He will have to pay a higher price for the things he must buy and there is nothing in this legislation providing that he will get a higher price for the things he has to sell.
It has been stated in the press, though as yet we have not heard it from the Prime Minister, that this legislation is not to apply immediately to agriculture, lumbering or fishing. I presume we will have to wait until we see the bill to find whether or not that is true. If this is to apply to the farmer as an employer then he is up against a double handicap. Not only that, but he is going to be handicapped in the labour market. To a very large extent the relief measures that have been adopted already have handicapped the farmer in that market. One of the effects of the establishment of relief camps has been to make it almost impossible for the farmer to get the help that he needs in order to carry on his work. The supply of farm labour is continually decreasing and becoming less and less efficient.
As I have said, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to offer opposition to the legislation now proposed, but I do want the house and the country to appreciate some of these effects which perhaps are not apparent to a great many people. I do not wish to discuss the 92582-19$
constitutional aspects of the question; I will leave that to the lawyers, but I think perhaps some of us who are not lawyers but who are in close touch with the actual facts and who know our own business can appreciate some of the practical difficulties involved in putting such a scheme into operation. I hope those practical difficulties may not be as great as they appear to me at the moment, but I want to tell the government that legislation of this kind will not be accepted as a substitute for the removal of trade restrictions and the doing of everything possible to facilitate world trade. At the very best, legislation of this kind is called for only because conditions are not what they ought to be, and it can only touch the fringe of the great problems confronting us. The real problems are the removal of trade barriers and, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) would) say, the question of finance. Tor my part I am inclined to agree with Cordell Hull, who said the other day that even if exchange were stabilized it would not remain stabilized for one hundred and twenty days unless trade restrictions were removed. At the moment, however, I will not discuss which of those two problems is the more important.
I should like to emphasize once more that the people whom I represent, and the great majority of the people on the prairies, cannot accept legislation of this kind as a substitute foi other legislation which we deem necessary in order to bring about the measures of relief that we feel the occasion demands.

The hon. member for Lisgar said that this measure would do something to keep the agricultural industry from getting cheap labour. That was the inference; why not be frank about it? I must absolutely disagree on that point. The hon. gentleman further suggested that the implementation of a policy of this description would cause people to be lazy. If the hon. member would read the evidence given before all the commissions appointed by British governments, whether Labour or Conservative, he would

find that it has been explicitly pointed out that the amount of malingering under the legislation there has been of no account whatever.
I am not going to speak at any length, because we are merely discussing the principle of the bill. I do not think this measure is intended to be a solution of our whole unemployment problem. To reach that solution we will have to find an entirely different approach, and in my personal opinion we will have to adopt entirely different legislation. There are two distinct problems. This bill is to deal with the question of unemployment and the payment of men out of work, through an insurance system. There will have to be different proposals. Of course the legislation is based on the English contributory system. I think we should point out further that under the proposed scheme the worker will receive sixty cents for his thirty cents. When the system in Great Britain was inaugurated twenty-one years ago it covered only seven trades involving little more than 2,000,000 employees.

speechtext:
I shall not enter into an argument about the figures; I think I am approximately correct. But to-day, after twenty-one years of experience and after twenty-eight major operations on the legislation, over 13,000,000 employees are operating under the English legislation. In the last three or four months they have reduced the age of insured persons from sixteen years to fourteen years, because the board school age in Great Britain is up to fourteen years. Within the last three months they have included agricultural workers within the range of this legislation. With these faots in mind we can see how there has been evolutionary development of this form of legislation. As time has gone on they have, as a result of their practical experience, broadened the range of those who may come under the legislation. I know it would be far better for me to spread all over the map, but it is my candid opinion that if we want to maintain this sort of legislation and if we wish to launch it soundly we must have a sound beginning and then broaden our operations as experience dictates.
I derive the greatest enjoyment from a contemplation of the fundamentals underlying the resolution before us, because it involves a redistribution of income. We will get a great deal more of that before we are through with the policies the Prime Minister has launched. He may not go as far as he

Unemployment Insurance
had expected to go, but the next government will have to act, whether they like it or not. Present conditions are a direct challenge to our democratic institutions, no matter whether we have a Conservative government, a Liberal government or a government composed of members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. We cannot overestimate or overlook the lessons taught by Europe in the last ten years. The will to live is the strongest instinct in a human being and one which is inevitably expressed in the nation. This is the direction in which mankind is moving; it may be the wrong direction, but undoubtedly that is the way it is going. The other fellow has fallen down on the job and mankind is trying this new tack.
I am not going to be critical, because I believe there is plenty of time for that when the bill is introduced and we are fully aware of what it contains. I believe at the present time we should act as though we were considering the measure from the standpoint of the benefits it may confer upon the Canadian people. I am well aware of the fact that relief measures must be distinct from unemployment insurance. I would remind the government however that it must not make the mistake of making insurance payments lower than the amount a man could get on relief. If that were done the legislation would fall to the ground. I should like to see the government include in the proposed scheme as many classes of working people as possible.
We have heard about the experience of other countries who have pioneered in this type of legislation and we would find it comparatively easy to profit from their experience. The hon. member for North Winnipeg spoke about labour exchanges. I understand they are used in Great Britain and are recommended in the country to the south of us. I should like to observe however that up to the present the only place where planning has been successful, so far as its effect upon human beings is concerned, has been in the prisons, the army, or the navy, where the same kind of clothes are worn by all.
Our approach to this problem must be in conformity with the desire of our people to come along with us. When this legislation is in operation I have no doubt the individualistic characteristics of the Canadian people will show themselves. I shall not say more at this time because I am discussing only the principle of the legislation, and shall reserve my criticisms of the bill until after its introduction.

It is to take care of those who are unemployed when they are unemployed. My hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) says: "To elect the government." Everyone has a right to his opinion. But we do know this, that once the law goes on the statute books in any country it is never repealed.
The Prime Minister took exception to the *statement of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) that nothing the Prime Minister had said1 would lead the public to believe that those who are unemployed to-day would not be included in the bill. I have before me the Vancouver Daily Province of January 5 giving a report of the Prime Minister's radio talk of January 4, and I find under the heading, Insurance to Replace Relief, the following report of the Prime Minister's remarks :
Now that we have achieved some measure of control over economic conditions and can cooperate without fear of imminent disaster, we are going to do away as quickly as possible with emei'gency relief measures and put in a permanent system of sound and scientific insurance against unemployment.
I claim that that is a definite statement that the purpose of the unemployment legislation to be brought before this parliament

was to substitute insurance for the relief measures that are in effect to-day. It means either that or nothing at all. I am quite satisfied that the Prime Minister's statement was very direct and very emphatic, but this resolution and the bill to be founded upon it does not touch that situation at all. The unemployment problem and the relief problem in this country are one. People are on relief because they are unemployed; and to make provision for those who are employed to-day against some period in the future when they may be unemployed is not touching today's unemployment problem.
Again, assuming that conditions are improving and that as we go on with these other reforms and when we get the Liberal government in power, things will boom once more, there will be no need for this unemployment insurance; but in the meantime those who are unemployed to-day are suffering, and there is nothing in this legislation that is going to be of any benefit to them.
That is the reason, Mr. Chairman, why I criticize this measure, although I am in favour of the principle of unemployment insurance, not because it is a solution for unemployment, but because so long as we have the capitalist sj'stem we shall have unemployment, for it is just as much a part of capitalism as profits. Every time profits are made, unemployment is created as well, so long as we maintain the capitalist system we should inaugurate and carry out measures to take care of the victims of that system, and a comprehensive system of unemployment insurance will do it, I believe, under the circumstances, better than any other way that we know of at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution that is before the Chair is, I take it, the first step in the inauguration of the government's new proposals for reform. May I first of all congratulate the government on what it has proposed to do? I shall, of course, reserve the right to criticize both the principle and the details of such legislation as may be brought down, but at this stage I think congratulations are due the government upon at least having turned its face in a new direction. I think that that is the most significant thing to be observed, not only in respect to this particular proposal, but in respect to the entire legislative program as outlined by the Prime Minister in his radio addresses.
It is strange that some people seem to be sorry that the government has turned its face from destruction and towards something sensible, but I have no criticism whatever in

Unemployment Insurance
that regard. The fact that the government has turned its face, or that the government have turned their faces-I am never sure whether we should speak of the government as an individual or collectively, but whatever may be the correct term, the government has turned its face in a new direction. That indicates first that the old methods that have been practised by governments in Canada and other governments in the world to meet the growing crises of the collapsing social order have been abandoned, at all events by this government, and have been abandoned because they proved to be inadequate. In the second place it indicates that the new economics which has been espoused from this comer of the house for thirteen years has at last found some justification. I do not know to what extent the proposed legislation will go, but certainly the government proposes to move in the direction which we in this section of the house have advocated for many years.
If I had any criticism at all to offer at this stage it would be in respect to the objective which the government may entertain. The question that is troubling my mind most is this: Does the government propose to try to repair capitalism by methods of this sort, or has it set its face towards the rebuilding of our economic system? I think that is the point that will determine the ultimate success of what the government is undertaking. So far as I am concerned I frankly say that I do not believe any government can successfully and adequately repair capitalism. I am quite convinced that the longer it goes on, the more serious conditions will become, and while I welcome these repair methods in so far as they may be able to alleviate human suffering during the process of getting wise enough to build a new system, nevertheless I do not desire to associate myself with the idea of repairing the capitalistic order. I believe we should begin to rebuild upon entirely new foundations, and however slowly we may go, every step we take should be towards that objective.
The resolution before the committee is a proposal in respect of unemployment insurance. The Prime Minister has explained t in a general way as sufficiently, I presume, as is necessary at this stage. It is an insurance proposal, and that being so, it must necessarily apply only to those who are qualified to come within the scope of its provisions. I do not believe much good can be accomplished by prolonging the discussion here. I think we should hasten to get the details of the bill and then to judge its merits from the actual
clauses of the legislation. But may I say that unemployment insurance has a very limited field, and that field becomes more restricted as the industrial system develops. The time for this legislation was twenty-five years ago. Then it would have done some good, for it would have built up a reserve which would have been of tremendous advantage to the Canadian wage workers during the past four years. The best time to insure a man against death is when he is alive. Now the government is being compelled by the pressure of events, by the threatening starvation of multitudes of the people, to introduce an insurance policy against unemployment at a time when unemployment is almost at its peak. That is like insuring people who already have tombstones at their heads. The government is faced with a difficulty. They had to do something to meet the situation, and while they felt that something had to be done, the economic conditions were inopportune for doing it.
This is perhaps one of the worst periods in the history of Canada for the introduction of such a measure as this, and yet it must be introduced. In that connection I think we ought to remind the opposition, in its criticisms of the measure, that in the years of great prosperity, when the Liberal party had power and when a measure of this sort could very well have been introduced, when its value would have been immeasurable, they did not do anything about it. Now we are faced with a very serious situation indeed and are compelled to take a step of this kind. But unemployment insurance-and this is the point I want to make-is inadequate in any country at any time to meet the industrial situation which has developed under the capitalist system. Personally I believe that the introduction of this principle will mark a beginning, if an inadequate one, in the right direction in so far as it will have meant, to a limited extent, the enabling of the working classes within its provisions to build up a reserve against the time when there will be no work for them to do. That may be extended indefinitely as the need develops, and so I say it is perhaps a beginning in the right direction.
But what we really need is insurance against being denied access to the abundance which mechanical invention and scientific methods of production have made available. And while, under a proposal of this sort, the government will make provision for the insurance of the workers of Canada, I would favour a system that would go much further than that and extend the principle to all the people of Canada, a system that would enable them to
Unemployment Insurance

have access to the abundance which our machinery and natural resources have made available. That is of course a matter of finance; it is a matter of using properly the national or social credit to provide purchasing power so that people may be able to buy the goods they produce. When the right time comes I shall be able to expound that theory further and perhaps move amendments in that connection if necessary. At the moment I only observe this, that there are many difficulties in the way of the government in bringing in legislation of this sort in Canada. There are difficulties to be faced in any country, and more perhaps in this coimtry than in any other. As I have already pointed out, the need of the moment is so great that action such as this is demanded; and yet conditions are inopportune for the inauguration of legislation of this sort. But in addition to that the government has to face certain difficulties in the matter of jurisdiction, with which other countries have not to contend.
I for one therefore propose to place no more difficulties in the path of the government than they have now. I want to congratulate them on what they have done and if they go any distance I will cheer them; if they go still further I will cheer them more, and if the opposition should make still more advanced proposals I should gladly commend them also. I do not care which government brings in legislation of this kind or legislation that has for its object meeting in any way, however small, the economic difficulties of our people at this time. Representatives of labour in Canada have asked for this legislation for nearly twenty-five years and this government Las been the first to undertake to provide it. Even if it is not all that we may expect, we welcome' it as a beginning, and shall look forward with great interest to the remaining portion of the government's program.

The resolution indicates
that a fairly comprehensive scheme of unemployment insurance is to be set up. Employees, employers and the dominion government will contribute to this scheme, and it would appear that the provincial governments are being largely left out of the picture. And yet we must remember that the provincial governments have been carrying on a great deal of the social work which has been done in this country. They have administered the Mothers' Allowances Act, the Old Age Pensions Act and particularly the Workmen's Compensation Act. They have therefore a great deal of information which would be of considerable use in carrying out the provisions of this proposed act. They have

statistics; they have trained staff; and the workmen's compensation boards in the various provinces have payrolls, so that they are in pretty close touch with the employers of labour and with the employees themselves within their respective territories. It would seem reasonable therefore that, instead of setting up an entirely new organization, these experienced people could be made use of and possibly the act administered by the workmen's compensation boards in the different provinces.
I quite agree with the last speaker that the people generally, particularly in Alberta, are looking for something much more comprehensive. Social credit has certainly taken a great hold in that province and in one town there has been erected a large wooden banner across the main street with the words Vote for Social Credit. I feel that many of these people will be looking for much that is more comprehensive than we have in this proposed measure.
I wish to commend one feature and that is the fact that it is contributory, because I believe that an employee who is contributing to a scheme is in a much better position than the employee who is receiving something to which he has not contributed. He has at least a contract and something that he can depend upon when he needs help.

Looking at the question, secondly, from a dominion point of view, may I read just a few lines from the report of the select standing committee on industrial and international relations in 1929 when dealing with the question of insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity. That question naturally brought up other questions akin to unemployment insurance, such as old age pensions and sickness insurance. The matter of social insurance came before the government in 1921 as a consequence of certain recommendations and conventions growing out of the international labour convention dealing with labour held at Washington in 1919. In 1921 the then Minister of Justice, Hon. C. J. Doherty, put forward his opinion of unemployment insurance based upon these recommendations and conventions of the Washington conference called by the international labour office of the League of Nations. The point of view put forward was this:
In this view-

-unemployment insurance has a pronounced federal aspect

-and on the whole the minister thinks the establishment of a system of unemployment insurance is competent to the dominion in the exercise of its residuary legislative powers with relation to the peace, order and good government of Canada.
That is another argument supplementing the one made by the Prime Minister when he quoted this afternoon from the constitution of Canada.
Thirdly, there is another and final thought and it is this-the provincial nngle. May I

Would you say that comes within that?

Well, I was going on to say that you could not bring it within peace, order and good government so long as it belongs to any of the enumerated items of section 92 -
Which of course defines the jurisdiction of the provinces. He goes on to say:
-and my own view' is that it is a subject which falls within the general designation of property and civil rights.

I am wondering whether it can or not; I am not going to say one thing or the other, but I expect the Prime Minister and those supporting him to come forward with further evidence to prove that from a constitutional point of view this question is wholly and entirely within the competency of the dominion government, that is, not solely within provincial jurisdiction.
